data.text/markdown:
Stullen-Statistik: better than GTA VI 🥪

A serious data analysis of a very unserious sandwich simulator. stulle.app is a German sandwich simulator. You pick a bread, spread something on it, drop toppings on top, and the result gets a serial number and a permalink. Every sandwich is also served as JSON at stulle.app/api/photos/{id}: the bread, each spread pass, and every topping with its position and rotation, in stacking order. The data comes from pipeline.py in the repo, which GitHub Actions runs every day: new sandwiches, recently banned or deleted ones, CLIP embeddings of the photos and a 2D map. It fetches IDs block by block so that coverage stays even, which means a partial scrape is a uniform random sample of all sandwiches. Names are given in German with the English in brackets.

data.text/markdown:
2 · The Spread Sheet

Bread and spread

3 · Jam Sessions & Wurst-Case Scenarios

What goes with what

Each cell compares two ingredients across all sandwiches.
  • Count: number of sandwiches that contain both.
  • Jaccard: |A∩B| / |A∪B|, so rare ingredients are on a fair footing.
  • Lift: P(A∩B) / (P(A)·P(B)). Red means they appear together more often than chance (a pairing), blue means less often (they avoid each other). Shown on a log₂ scale. Raw lift is red almost everywhere, because a long tail of "kitchen-sink" Stullen contains nearly every ingredient.
  • Lift (size-adjusted), the default: the same ratio, but chance is computed among sandwiches with the same number of distinct ingredients. This answers "given that someone uses 3 ingredients, are these two picked together more than chance?"
Order. By group (the default) puts spreads first, then savory, vegetables, junk and sweet, with the colour strip marking each block. Red squares inside a block mean a group sticks together; blue squares between blocks mean two groups avoid each other. By similarity uses hierarchical clustering on Jaccard similarity instead, so the data decides what sits next to what.

5 · Let's Go Ham

How common are the classics?

A sandwich counts as a classic only on a strict match: the defining toppings, plus at most the usual garnish, and nothing else. A Käsebrot with gummy bears on top does not count. The rules are in stulle/model.py (FAMOUS) and in the dataset's catalog.json.

data.text/markdown:
6 · Stairway to Leberkäse

How tall do they get?

The API records where each piece was dropped and in what order, but not where it came to rest. Height is therefore estimated from two simple models that bracket the truth:
  • Rigid stack (upper bound): each piece lands on the highest point under its footprint, as if nothing slides or nests.
  • Packed (lower bound): total topping volume divided by covered area, i.e. the whole pile squashed flat with no air.
Height is the geometric mean of the two. Against the photos of three towers (#7646 fries, #8939 chips, #36045) it lands within about 20% of what you can see. Topping sizes and thicknesses come from the app's own physics table. The bread itself is not included.

7 · The Lay of the Ham

When were they made, and from where?

data.text/html: Before Sat 21 Nov, 14:00 Berlin time the counter barely moves: 230 sampled sandwiches (IDs up to ~236) between 29 Oct and launch, which looks like pre-launch testing. After that it runs at hundreds to thousands per hour.

data.text/markdown:
9 · Hand-Me-Down Sandwiches

Remixes

Weiterbelegen ("keep topping") loads someone else's Stulle into your editor, and the result records it as parentId. Following parents back gives remix chains.

data.text/html: 8.8% of sandwiches are remixes. When both the remix and its parent are in the sample (4,265 pairs), the remix adds a median of 0 pieces. The longest chain found in the sample is 11 hops.Most-remixed Stullen (counts are within the sample)

data.text/markdown:
12 · CLIP Art

Searching the photos by meaning

The JSON says what is on a Stulle, not what it looks like. Spreads in particular are free-hand brush strokes, and people use them to draw, write slogans, and paint flags. To find those we embed every thumbnail with CLIP ViT-L/14, a model trained to put images and their descriptions close together. Then we can search the photos with plain text, sort every photo into a rough taxonomy, and lay them all out on a map. The pipeline embeds every photo with CLIP ViT-L/14 and precomputes the census, the preset searches and the map, so all of this also works in the browser. Free-text search needs the CLIP text model, so it appears only where the notebook runs on a real Python server (locally, or on molab).
50,024 photos embedded (100% of the sandwiches in the sample).

data.text/markdown:
Method notes (the crusts: boring, but they hold it together)

  • Source. GET https://stulle.app/api/photos/{id} for every ID up to the newest one listed on /alle. 404s are deleted or reported sandwiches. The scraper is throttled to about 2–3 requests per second and backs off when it gets an HTTP 429.
  • Sampling. IDs are fetched in shuffled order, so until the scrape finishes every percentage here is an estimate from a uniform random sample. Absolute counts (pieces placed, remix counts) only cover the sample.
  • Spreads. A spread is "used" if it was picked at least once. The brush strokes are dropped when scraping; only their count is kept.
  • Physics. Topping diameters and thicknesses come from the app's JS bundle. The bread is 11 cm across.
